Optimise graph-based multiple testing procedures for a group sequential design

Source: R/optimisation_gsd.R
graph_optimise_gsd.Rd

Group sequential counterpart of graph_optimise(). Optimise the hypothesis weights and transition matrix of a graph-based multiple testing procedure for a design with several analyses, using nloptr::nloptr() local optimisation and, optionally, a genetic algorithm using GA::ga() for global optimisation.

Usage

graph_optimise_gsd(
  pvals,
  graph_constraint,
  trial_success,
  ...,
  alpha = NULL,
  stopping_rule = NULL,
  start_graph = list(list(hyp_weight = NULL, trans_matrix = NULL)),
  global_search = TRUE,
  num_threads = 1L,
  control = multigrain_control(),
  verbose = multigrain_verbosity()
)

Arguments

pvals

A multigrain_pvals_gsd object of repeated (or, per hypothesis, sequential) p-values, created with transform_pvalues_gsd(), or a multigrain_pvals_gsd_spec object, created by transform_pvalues_gsd() when one or more spending functions are sf_hsd_opt(), to optimise those spending parameters with the graph (see Details).

graph_constraint

A multigrain_graph_constraint object containing constraints on the graph's weights and transition matrix. Created with graph_constraint().

trial_success

A multigrain_trial_success_gsd object defining the trial success measure (gain function) to maximise. Created with trial_success_gsd(). A fixed-sample object from trial_success() is not accepted; write a rejection-only gain such as r1 + r2 with trial_success_gsd() instead.

...

These dots are for future extensions and must be empty.

alpha

A single numeric value representing the overall one-sided significance level, or NULL (the default) to use the level of pvals. A supplied value must be greater than 0 and at most the level the repeated p-values were built up to: above that they are capped at 1, so no allocation beyond it could ever reject.

stopping_rule

A multigrain_stopping_rule_gsd object from stopping_rule_gsd(), or NULL (the default) for a trial that runs to its final analysis unless it rejects every hypothesis earlier.

start_graph

Optional. Initial list of graphs suggested. Each graph is defined as a list containing starting weight vector hyp_weight and transition matrix trans_matrix. If NULL, default starting values are generated (currently with a Bonferroni-Holm graph).

global_search

A logical indicating whether to perform a global optimisation before the local optimisation. Defaults to TRUE.

num_threads

Number of threads to use for parallel execution of the shortcut algorithm. On shared systems (HPC clusters, login nodes), always explicitly set num_threads based on your resource allocation. Default is 1L (serial execution).

control

An optional multigrain_control object can be used to set various graph optimisation parameters. Created with multigrain_control().

verbose

An optional string controlling verbosity ("detail" > "info" > "silent"). Verbosity can also be set at package level with the multigrain_verbosity option (see multigrain_verbosity()):

  • "info" (default): will only show milestones / informational messages highlighting the progress of the optimisation at coarse-grained level.

  • "detail": will show milestones and information about fine-grained optimisation events.

  • "silent": no information about the progress of the optimisation is printed to the console. Errors and warnings are still thrown normally.

Value

A multigrain_graph_optimal object containing:

  • hyp_weight: Optimised hypothesis weights (numeric vector).

  • trans_matrix: Optimised transition matrix (numeric matrix).

  • constraints: List of constraints used in the optimisation for weights and transition matrix.

  • trial_success: The trial success function used in the optimisation.

  • power: The calc_power_pvals_gsd() list for the optimised graph, so it carries power by analysis, the decision-time distribution and the value of the trial success measure as well as the fixed-sample power metrics.

  • solution: A list containing:

    • opt_source: Source of the optimal solution (local or global).

    • graph_valid: Named logical vector indicating validity of the local and global solutions (c("local" = TRUE/FALSE, "global" = TRUE/FALSE)).

  • global_search: TRUE or FALSE indicating whether a global optimisation was performed.

  • control: A modified multigrain_control() object used. The values passed on by the user are complemented with contextual defaults.

  • global_output: Output from the genetic algorithm if global optimisation was performed.

  • local_output: Output from the NLOPT optimisation.

  • start_graph: Initial starting values used in the optimisation.

  • stopping_rule: the rule, when one was supplied.

When pvals is a spending spec, also:

  • spending_param: the chosen value of each spending parameter (named numeric vector; the names are the ids of sf_hsd_opt(), else gamma, or gamma1, gamma2, ... when there are several).

  • hyp_spending_param: the value per hypothesis, NA for a hypothesis with fixed spending or one whose single analysis at full information makes spending irrelevant.

  • spending: a spending label per hypothesis, such as sfHSD(param = -0.25) for a tagged one.

  • spending_bounds, spending_step: the bounds (a matrix with one row per parameter) and the lattice step of each parameter.

  • spending_group: the parameter of each hypothesis, an integer index into spending_param (NA for none).

  • spending_profile: the warm-started profile (see Details), a data frame with columns param, value, gain, gain_fixed_graph, diff, se and n_eval (the number of COBYLA evaluations at that node), and the graph of each row as the attribute graphs.

  • spending_search: the genetic algorithm's coverage of each lattice, a data frame with columns param, value, visits and best_fitness_subsample, the best gain seen at that node on the algorithm's subsample, which is not comparable with the profile's gains. All NA without a global search.

  • profile_converged: FALSE when, with two or more parameters, the rounds of the profile did not settle within three, or when a node of a final recomputed profile beats the chosen value (a negative diff); the plateaus are then indicative.

Details

The output is a graph where a specified objective function - the trial success measure - is maximised under given constraints on the graph structure, conditional on the repeated p-values supplied. Because the gain sees the analysis at which each hypothesis was rejected, an early rejection can be worth more than a late one.

The search, the encoding and the pruning are those of graph_optimise(). Only the evaluation changes: the group sequential kernel runs the fixed-sample cascade once per analysis, carrying the updated graph forward, and reports the analysis at which each hypothesis was declared rejected. Those decision times are what trial_success scores.

With a stopping rule the kernel stops each simulated trial at the first interim whose condition holds, so the gain and every reported power see only the rejections made before the trial stopped; a trial that rejects every hypothesis stops at that analysis in any case.

Optimised spending parameters. When pvals is a spending spec, from transform_pvalues_gsd() with one or more sf_hsd_opt() entries, the Hwang-Shih-DeCani parameter of each tagged group is chosen jointly with the graph. Every value the search can try is a node of the parameter's lattice (the multiples of step inside bounds), and every node's boundary table was built and checked for well ordering when the spec was created, so the chosen design controls the error rate as any fixed choice would. The search has two stages:

  • the global stage runs the genetic algorithm on the graph genes with one gene per spending parameter appended, each mapped to a lattice node, on the nsim_global subsample. The repeated p-values of that subsample are computed once at every node. The default population size counts each parameter as one more hypothesis;

  • the local stage refines the graph by COBYLA at the genetic algorithm's parameter values, then walks each parameter's lattice outward from there and re-optimises the graph at every node, starting COBYLA from the best of the current optimum's graph, the previous node's graph and the best graph the genetic algorithm found at that node (a warm-started profile). It moves to the best node; with two or more parameters the sweep is repeated until no parameter moves, at most three rounds. Every gain of this stage is computed on one ordering of the simulated trials, so differences between nodes are paired.

The profile is returned as spending_profile: for every node of each parameter, with the other parameters held at their chosen values, the gain with the graph re-optimised (gain), the gain of the chosen graph kept fixed (gain_fixed_graph), the paired difference from the optimum (diff) and its batch-means standard error over 100 blocks of trials (se). At the chosen value gain equals gain_fixed_graph and diff and se are 0. print() condenses the profile to two plateaus: the connected run of nodes around the chosen value whose diff is at most 5e-4, and the same run for the fixed-graph gain, measured from its largest value. A wide plateau means the parameter hardly matters for this design within that range; the fixed-graph plateau is narrower when the best graph depends on the parameter. summary() prints the table and the number of nodes the genetic algorithm visited.

As on the fixed path, the better of the two stages' graphs is kept, each scored on the full sample at its own parameter values. If the genetic algorithm's graph is kept, its parameter values are reported and the profile is still the local stage's, which started from them. Unlike the fixed path, a start_graph is honoured when global_search = FALSE.

The parameters and the graph are chosen on the same simulated trials that score them, so the reported gain is optimistic (the winner's curse), a little more so than for the graph alone. To check the design, simulate fresh p-values, build a spec from them with the same spending, and evaluate the chosen graph with calc_power_pvals_gsd() on resolve_pvalues_gsd(new_spec, result$spending_param).

The boundary tables are the main cost of building a spec: about 0.9 s per lattice node at the default grid_size = 1024 with two analyses, about 20 s for the default 21-node lattice. grid_size = 512 halves this; in the package's measurements its largest relative interpolation error against grid_size = 1024 was 8.2e-6. A spec can be reused across gains and stopping rules on the same draws.

See also

graph_optimise() for the fixed-sample version, transform_pvalues_gsd() for the p-value object and trial_success_gsd() for the gain.

Examples

# two hypotheses, an interim at 50% information and a final analysis
corr <- matrix(c(1, 0.5, 0.5, 1), nrow = 2)

set.seed(1)
raw <- simulate_pvalues_gsd(
    power_nominal = c(0.9, 0.8),
    corr_matrix = corr,
    info_frac = c(0.5, 1),
    nsim = 2000
)

pvals <- transform_pvalues_gsd(
    raw,
    spending = gsDesign::sfLDOF,
    grid_size = 128L
)

# a rejection at the final analysis is worth 75% of one at the interim
gain <- trial_success_gsd(
    r1 * d(t1) + r2 * d(t2),
    d = c(1, 0.75)
)
#> ✔ Trial success function compiled and sourced successfully.

# \donttest{
result <- graph_optimise_gsd(
    pvals = pvals,
    graph_constraint = graph_constraint_free(2),
    trial_success = gain,
    stopping_rule = stopping_rule_gsd(r1),
    num_threads = 2
)
#> ℹ Running global optimization

#> 
#> ℹ Evaluating trial success of globally optimised graph

#> ✔ Pruning redundant weights and edges [8ms]
#> 
#> ℹ Evaluating trial success of pruned graph
#> ✔ Evaluating trial success of pruned graph [6ms]

# choose the spending parameter of H2 jointly with the graph
spec <- transform_pvalues_gsd(
    raw,
    spending = list(gsDesign::sfLDOF, sf_hsd_opt(bounds = c(-4, 0))),
    grid_size = 128L
)
result_spending <- graph_optimise_gsd(
    pvals = spec,
    graph_constraint = graph_constraint_free(2),
    trial_success = gain,
    stopping_rule = stopping_rule_gsd(r1),
    num_threads = 2
)
